about: "Make it specific" prompts for Unit 3 (docs/apprecalc-architecture.md, "Make it specific"): the reasoning the scoring guidelines reward, with an answer that earns the point, one that misses it and a part-by-part builder. Every number is recomputed in JUSTIFY_NUMBERS (scripts/lib/apprecalc-exams.mjs).

prompts.title: b from the period
prompts.context: A buoy bobs up and down, repeating its motion every $8$ seconds. Its height is modeled by $h(t) = 3\sin(bt) + 5$ meters, $t$ seconds after it passes the midline going up, with $b > 0$.
checklist: Says the period of $\sin(bt)$ is $\frac{2\pi}{b}$
Sets $\frac{2\pi}{b} = 8$ and solves: $b = \frac{2\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4}$

earns.answer: The period of $3\sin(bt) + 5$ is $\frac{2\pi}{b}$. The motion repeats every $8$ seconds, so $\frac{2\pi}{b} = 8$ and $b = \frac{2\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4}$.
earns.why: It links b to the period with the formula and the given value, and gives b exactly.

misses.answer: The motion repeats every $8$ seconds, so $b = 8$.
misses.why: b is not the period; it is 2π divided by the period.

why.1: b stretches the graph horizontally; the period is 2π divided by it.
why.2: This is the frequency, cycles per second.

why.1: 8 is the period, not b; b = 2π/8.

prompts.title: The phase shift, factored first
prompts.prompt: Describe the horizontal shift that takes the graph of $y = 2\sin(3t) - 1$ to the graph of $g$, and explain how you know.
checklist: Factors the $3$: $3t + \frac{\pi}{2} = 3\left(t + \frac{\pi}{6}\right)$
Reads the shift from $t + \frac{\pi}{6}$: left by $\frac{\pi}{6}$
Says why $\frac{\pi}{2}$ is not the shift: it is $3$ times the shift

earns.answer: Factor the $3$ inside: $3t + \frac{\pi}{2} = 3\left(t + \frac{\pi}{6}\right)$, so $g(t) = 2\sin\left(3\left(t + \frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right) - 1$. Replacing $t$ by $t + \frac{\pi}{6}$ shifts the graph of $y = 2\sin(3t) - 1$ left by $\frac{\pi}{6}$. The $\frac{\pi}{2}$ is not the shift: it is $3$ times the shift.
earns.why: It factors before reading the shift, gives its size and direction, and names the trap.

misses.answer: The graph shifts $\frac{\pi}{2}$ to the right.
misses.why: Both the size and the direction are wrong: factor out b first, and t + c shifts the graph left.

why.1: 3 times π/2 is 3π/2, not π/2.
why.2: Factor 3 out of both terms: π/2 ÷ 3 = π/6.

why.1: t + π/6 moves the graph left; t − π/6 would move it right.

prompts.title: Five points from a context
prompts.context: A Ferris wheel has its center $18$ meters above the ground and a radius of $15$ meters. It turns once every $40$ seconds. A rider boards at the lowest point at $t = 0$.
prompts.prompt: Give the coordinates $(t, h)$ of the minimum, the midline crossings and the maximum of the rider's height during the first turn, and say what each point is.
checklist: Minimums at $(0, 3)$ and $(40, 3)$: $18 - 15 = 3$ meters, at the start and end of a turn
Midline crossings at $(10, 18)$ going up and $(30, 18)$ going down, a quarter turn from each extreme
Maximum at $(20, 33)$: $18 + 15 = 33$ meters, half a turn after boarding

earns.answer: The lowest height is $18 - 15 = 3$ meters, at $(0, 3)$ and again at $(40, 3)$, the minimums. A quarter turn later, at $t = 10$, the rider is level with the center: $(10, 18)$, a midline crossing going up. At half a turn, $t = 20$, the rider is at the top: $(20, 33)$, the maximum, $18 + 15 = 33$ meters. At $t = 30$ the rider passes the midline going down: $(30, 18)$.
earns.why: Each point is labeled as a minimum, maximum or midline crossing, with coordinates from the context: center, radius and period.

misses.answer: The height goes from $0$ to $33$ and back down, with the middle at $16.5$.
misses.why: The rider boards 3 meters up, not at the ground; the midline is the center height, 18, and no times are given.

why.1: The bottom of the wheel is 18 − 15 = 3 meters above the ground.
At t = 40 the rider is back at the bottom.
why.2: At t = 10 the rider is a quarter turn up, level with the center.

prompts.title: Decreasing, with the rate of change increasing
prompts.context: Let $h(t) = 5\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}t\right) + 10$. On $(2, 4)$ the graph goes from the midline, $h(2) = 10$, down to the minimum, $h(4) = 5$.
prompts.prompt: Determine whether, on the interval $(2, 4)$, $h$ is increasing or decreasing and whether the rate of change of $h$ is increasing or decreasing. Give a reason for each.
checklist: Says $h$ is decreasing on $(2, 4)$, from $h(2) = 10$ down to the minimum $h(4) = 5$
Compares rates over equal intervals: on $[2, 3]$ about $-3.536$, on $[3, 4]$ about $-1.464$, so the graph is concave up
Concludes the rate of change of $h$ is increasing on $(2, 4)$: negative, and getting closer to $0$

earns.answer: $h$ is decreasing on $(2, 4)$: it falls from $h(2) = 10$ at the midline to the minimum $h(4) = 5$. Over equal intervals, $h(3) = 5\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) + 10 \approx 6.464$, so the average rate of change is about $\frac{6.464 - 10}{3 - 2} = -3.536$ on $[2, 3]$ and about $\frac{5 - 6.464}{4 - 3} = -1.464$ on $[3, 4]$. The rates are negative and increasing toward $0$, so the graph is concave up on $(2, 4)$ and the rate of change of $h$ is increasing there, as the graph levels off into the minimum.
earns.why: It treats h and its rate of change as two questions, with a reason for each tied to values on the interval: the rates over two equal intervals show the concavity.

misses.answer: $h$ is decreasing on $(2, 4)$, so its rate of change is decreasing too.
misses.why: A decreasing function can have an increasing rate of change; here the graph flattens into the minimum, so the rate rises toward 0.

why.1: h goes from 10 down to 5.

rate.label: The rate of change of h is
options: increasing, because the graph is concave up

why.1: The direction of h does not decide how its rate changes; concavity does.

prompts.title: Tangent near its asymptote
prompts.context: To three decimal places, $\tan(1.5) \approx 14.101$ and $\tan(1.65) \approx -12.599$, with angles in radians.
prompts.prompt: Describe the behavior of $\tan x$ on each side of $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$ using limit notation, and explain why the graph has a vertical asymptote there.
checklist: Says $\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0$ while $\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1$, so $\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ is undefined and unbounded there
Writes $\lim_{x \to \pi/2^-} \tan x = \infty$, matching $\tan(1.5) \approx 14.101$
Writes $\lim_{x \to \pi/2^+} \tan x = -\infty$, matching $\tan(1.65) \approx -12.599$

earns.answer: $\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, and at $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$, $\cos x = 0$ while $\sin x = 1$, so the quotient is undefined and its size grows without bound nearby: a vertical asymptote. Just left of $\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\cos x$ is small and positive, so $\lim_{x \to \pi/2^-} \tan x = \infty$ (for example $\tan(1.5) \approx 14.101$). Just right, $\cos x$ is small and negative, so $\lim_{x \to \pi/2^+} \tan x = -\infty$ (for example $\tan(1.65) \approx -12.599$).
earns.why: Both one-sided limits are written with their signs, each with a reason and a value that supports it.

misses.answer: $\tan x$ goes to infinity at $\frac{\pi}{2}$ because $\cos x$ is zero.
misses.why: It gives neither side nor sign, and the two sides go in opposite directions.

why.1: Left of π/2, sine and cosine are both positive.
why.2: tan(π/4) = 1; near π/2 the values are huge, like 14.101 at x = 1.5.

why.1: Right of π/2, cosine is negative, so the quotient is negative: tan(1.65) ≈ −12.599.

prompts.title: Inverse sine and its range
prompts.prompt: Find the exact value of $\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)$, and explain why it is not $\frac{5\pi}{6}$.
checklist: Evaluates the inside first: $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$
Uses the range of inverse sine, $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$: $\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{6}$
Says $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ is outside that range, so it cannot be an output of $\sin^{-1}$

earns.answer: First, $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$. Inverse sine gives the angle in $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ whose sine is $\frac{1}{2}$, which is $\frac{\pi}{6}$. So $\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}$. It is not $\frac{5\pi}{6}$, because $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ is outside the range of inverse sine.
earns.why: It works from the inside out and names the range that decides the answer.

misses.answer: They cancel, so the answer is $\frac{5\pi}{6}$.
misses.why: Inverse sine undoes sine only on [−π/2, π/2]; 5π/6 is outside that range.

why.1: 5π/6 is in the second quadrant, where sine is positive.
why.2: That is the size of cos(5π/6).

why.1: 5π/6 is not in [−π/2, π/2], the range of inverse sine.

prompts.title: Every solution in an interval
prompts.prompt: Solve $2\cos x + \sqrt{3} = 0$ for $0 \le x < 2\pi$. Give every solution exactly.
checklist: Isolates the cosine: $\cos x = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
Finds the reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$ and the quadrants where cosine is negative, II and III
Gives both solutions, $x = \frac{5\pi}{6}$ and $x = \frac{7\pi}{6}$, and no others

earns.answer: $2\cos x = -\sqrt{3}$, so $\cos x = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. The reference angle is $\frac{\pi}{6}$, and cosine is negative in quadrants II and III. So $x = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}$ and $x = \pi + \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{7\pi}{6}$, the two solutions in $[0, 2\pi)$.
earns.why: It finds every solution in the interval, exactly, with the quadrant reasoning shown.

misses.why: Inverse cosine gives one angle; cosine has the same value in quadrant III, so the second solution, 7π/6, is missed.

why.1: Moving √3 across makes it negative.
Cosine is also negative in quadrant III.

prompts.title: Down to one trigonometric function
prompts.prompt: Rewrite $\frac{\sin(2x)}{1 + \cos(2x)}$ as a single trigonometric function of $x$, for values of $x$ where both are defined. Show the identities you use.
checklist: Uses $\sin(2x) = 2\sin x \cos x$
Uses $\cos(2x) = 2\cos^2 x - 1$, so $1 + \cos(2x) = 2\cos^2 x$
Simplifies $\frac{2\sin x \cos x}{2\cos^2 x} = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \tan x$, one function

earns.answer: $\sin(2x) = 2\sin x \cos x$ and $\cos(2x) = 2\cos^2 x - 1$, so $1 + \cos(2x) = 2\cos^2 x$. Then $\frac{\sin(2x)}{1 + \cos(2x)} = \frac{2\sin x \cos x}{2\cos^2 x} = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \tan x$, a single trigonometric function.
earns.why: Each identity is named as a step, and the work goes all the way to one function, tan x, as the question asks.

misses.why: A quotient of sine and cosine is two functions; stopping here loses the point for a single trigonometric function.

identity.label: Which form of cos(2x)
options: cos²x − sin²x, left as it is

why.1: This leaves two functions in the denominator; the 2cos²x − 1 form lets the 1 cancel.
why.2: This is a true identity, but 1 + cos(2x) becomes 2 − 2sin²x, which does not cancel with the top.

why.1: That is still two functions; write it as tan x.
why.2: cot x is cos x over sin x, the reciprocal of the answer.

prompts.title: An average rate of change of r
prompts.prompt: Find the average rate of change of $r$ on $\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and explain what it tells you about the curve.
checklist: Computes $\frac{r(\pi/2) - r(0)}{\pi/2 - 0} = \frac{3 - 2}{\pi/2} = \frac{2}{\pi}$, about $0.637$
Names the slope of the secant line through $(0, 2)$ and $\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 3\right)$ on the graph of $r$ against $\theta$
Interprets it: on average the distance from the origin grows by about $0.637$ for each radian $\theta$ turns

earns.answer: The average rate of change of $r$ on $\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ is $\frac{r(\pi/2) - r(0)}{\pi/2 - 0} = \frac{3 - 2}{\pi/2} = \frac{2}{\pi} \approx 0.637$, the slope of the secant line through $(0, 2)$ and $\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 3\right)$ on the graph of $r$ against $\theta$. On average, the distance from the origin to the curve increases by about $0.637$ for each radian $\theta$ increases on this interval.
earns.why: It shows the quotient with values, names the secant line, and interprets the rate as a change in distance from the origin per radian.

misses.answer: $r$ goes from $2$ to $3$, so the rate is $1$.
misses.why: The change in r is not divided by the change in θ, π/2, and nothing names the secant line or what r measures.

why.1: This is the change in r; divide by the change in θ.
why.2: The change in r goes on top.

meaning.label: It means
options: the distance from the origin grows about 0.637 per radian, on average
the curve is 0.637 units from the origin

why.1: r is the distance; its average rate of change compares a change in r with a change in θ.

prompts.title: Radian mode and every solution
prompts.prompt: Solve $4\sin t = 1$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$, giving each solution correct to three decimal places. Explain how the calculator is used.
checklist: Uses radian mode: $\sin^{-1}(0.25) \approx 0.253$
Finds the second solution, $\pi - \sin^{-1}(0.25) \approx 2.889$, using the stored value
Gives both solutions to three decimal places, not degrees

earns.answer: $\sin t = 0.25$. In radian mode, $t = \sin^{-1}(0.25) \approx 0.253$. Sine has the same value at $\pi - t$, so with the stored value $t = \pi - \sin^{-1}(0.25) \approx 2.889$. Both are in $[0, \pi]$: $t \approx 0.253$ and $t \approx 2.889$.
earns.why: Radian mode, the stored value, and both solutions in the interval, each to three decimal places.

misses.why: This is in degrees, outside [0, π] in radians, and the second solution is missed.

why.1: The interval is in radians; degree mode gives 14.478, not an angle in [0, π].
Sine is positive in quadrant II too: π − 0.253 ≈ 2.889.
why.2: This is the angle in degrees; the interval is in radians.
